To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Caspase-1, caspase 4/11, and caspase 5 are important for growth inhibition of cytosolically replicating Salmonella Typhymurium in mouse macrophages and human epithelial cells.
caspases-1 and caspas-11 are not only involved in the activation of pyroptotic cell death but also in the inhibition of bacterial growth in the host cell cytosole.

caspase-8, caspase1 and caspases-4/5 (caspases-11) have important functions beyond their well-established role in host cell death and proinflammatory responses in the control of bacterial growth and elimination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of caspase activation in the control of bacterial growth and host cell death.
the molecular basis of the innate immune response to intracellular bacterial pathogens, in particular Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurim.
the role of caspase activation in the host response to cytosolic Salmonellae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
caspase- 1 and casp-11 are required to control bacterial growth in the cytosolic environment of mammalian host cells.
caspase-3, -4, -11, and -5 have important roles in the control of intracellular bacterial infection.
caspase-8, caspase1, and caspase11 are all involved in the control of bacterial growth, with caspase1 and caspases being involved in the initiation of pyroptotic death.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NOD-like receptors and caspase activation can be viewed as an early warning system that detects cytosolic bacteria, and triggers a variety of host defense mechanisms to control bacterial growth.

caspase-3, caspase 4/11, and caspase 1 are not just involved in pyroptosis, but also in growth inhibition of cytosolically located Salmonella.
